Tools & recommendations

Travel resources

Everything I actually use and trust — from gear I've carried across 40+ countries to apps I open every single trip.

✈

Getting There

Google Flights

Free

Still the best way to scout flight prices. I use the explore map to find where's cheap from my city at any given time.

Visit →

Skyscanner

Free

Better than Google Flights for obscure budget carriers and multi-city routes in less common regions.

Visit →

Rome2Rio

Free

Invaluable for overland travel — shows every way to get between two points including trains, buses, ferries and driving time.

Visit →

Seat61

Free

The definitive guide to train and ferry travel worldwide. Written by one obsessive person. More reliable than any official rail website.

Visit →
🏨

Accommodation

Booking.com

Free

My default for hotels and guesthouses. The free cancellation filter is the most useful feature — book early, cancel if plans change.

Visit →

Hostelworld

Free

Better hostel inventory than Booking. The review system is more detailed and I trust it more for solo travel.

Visit →

Airbnb

Free

Useful for apartments on longer stays, particularly in Eastern Europe and Latin America where it tends to be better value.

Visit →

Workaway

Paid

How I've stayed for free in exchange for a few hours of work per day. Life-changing for extended slow travel.

Visit →
📱

Apps I Actually Use

Maps.me

Free

Offline maps that work without data. I download every country before I arrive. Saved me more times than I can count.

Visit →

Airalo

Paid

eSIM marketplace. I buy a local data plan before landing and never deal with airport SIM stalls. Covers almost every country now.

Visit →

Notion

Free / Paid

Where I build all my trip planning docs, packing lists, and day-by-day itineraries. The offline app has gotten good enough to use in the field.

Visit →

XE Currency

Free

The one currency converter that works offline and doesn't try to add features I don't want. Simple and reliable.

Visit →
🎒

Gear I Travel With

Osprey Farpoint 40

Gear

My main bag for the last three years. Fits in carry-on overhead bins on most airlines, comfortable hip belt for long carry days.

View →

Peak Design Capture

Gear

Clips my camera to my bag strap for quick access. Worth it if you hate putting your camera away and missing shots.

View →

Anker PowerCore 26800

Gear

Charges my phone 7–8 times. I bring this on every trip. Bulky but I've never regretted it on a long travel day.

The only travel card that gives real exchange rates with no hidden markup. I use it everywhere and convert currencies in the app when the rate is good.

The person behind the passport

Hi! I'm Kevin.

My friends kept asking me for travel recommendations so… I created this blog instead! I'm a travel enthusiast & backpacker based out of San Francisco, CA. On Getawayguide, I write detailed getaway guides based on my firsthand travel experiences.

Whether it's your next 2 week vacation or 6 month sabbatical, my guides are here to help! Getawayguide is where I write about what I actually found — the best beaches, pristine alpine lakes, once in a lifetime experiences, most memorable hostels or the boring travel logistics.

59Countries visited
6Continents explored
1Bag. Always carry-on.

How this started

In 2023, I left my job in investment banking with no real plan. A week later, I found myself on a flight to Istanbul with nothing but my wallet, passport and a small backpack. I had never actually traveled solo before and was anxious about what came next.

It was a wild ride. I've squeezed myself into Ryanair seats, slept in less than ideal places, introduced myself to countless strangers (and set my savings account on fire in the process). With the discomfort came the most incredible experiences. I've visited places that I've only dreamed of and even more beautiful places I didn't even know existed.

I met the most amazing, unique people from every corner of the world. I would land in a country, not knowing a single soul and leave with a new group of friends. I've heard the most insane life stories and explored different cultures.

My love of travel didn't end there. Since then, I've gone on many trips (and the destination list keeps growing…). I keep getting asked for travel recommendations so I created this blog to help share them. I invest countless hours in meticulous research and planning before each trip. On my trips, I love documenting and taking photos.

How I travel

I've done every type of travel: 5 star resorts, dingy hostels and weekend international trips. My preference right now is solo backpacking. There's a thrill to it that can't be matched! Almost always overland when possible — I've taken more buses than I can count, a lot of slow overnight trains, a few cargo boats. I stay in a mix of hostels, guesthouses and hotels. I try to eat the local foods and immerse myself in the cultures.

Not every country is my favorite. The blog is a record of that. Not a highlight reel. There is nothing worse than reading an SEO optimized travel blog with no real content, AI slop and full of affiliate links. I aim to write honest guides about what a place is really like to travel in — costs, safety, logistics, the things traditional travel guides leave out. I write about the things that go wrong as much as the things that go right.

What I'm working on

Honestly, I have zero expectations for this travel blog. If 1 person reads it and it helps them with their next trip, then amazing. This is just a side project to document my travels, practice writing articles and learn some web design in the process.

Right now I'm slowly building out the destination guides — each country page will eventually have a full write-up with itineraries, logistics, and recommended reads. It's a long project. Subscribe to the newsletter if you want to know when new ones land.

Currently in

Home — San Francisco 🏠🌉

Next up

Balkans (May 2026)

Favourite trip so far

New Zealand, without question. Some of the most amazing hikes and landscapes. It seriously felt like you were on a different planet.

Biggest travel mistake

Boarding a bus in Kosovo while hungover with 5€ and falling asleep through the border crossing to Albania.

Destinations › Americas › Central America

El Salvador

Now is the best time to visit El Salvador before it becomes the tourism hotspot! It offers stunning waterfalls, great beaches for surfing and historic colonial towns, but still remains untouched by mass tourism.

Places to visit
El Salvador

1–2 Weeks In El Salvador: A Complete Backpacking Itinerary

A Complete Travel Guide and Backpacking Route

Find Cheap Flights To El Salvador Compare all airlines
Find Hostels in El Salvador Best budget stays
Book Excursions Tours & experiences
Find Transport in El Salvador Buses, shuttles & more
City Guide

The Ultimate Guide to Santa Ana, El Salvador's Second City

Hiking

The 7 Waterfalls Hike: El Salvador's Most Spectacular Trail

Beaches

El Tunco & El Zonte: The Best Surf Beaches in El Salvador

Towns

Suchitoto: A Guide to El Salvador's Most Beautiful Colonial Town

Planning

When to Visit

The best time to visit El Salvador is during the dry season, which runs from November through April. Skies are clear, roads are accessible, and the surf is consistent along the Pacific coast. The rainy season (May–October) brings lush green landscapes and far fewer tourists — a worthwhile trade-off if you don't mind the occasional afternoon downpour. December and January are the busiest months, so book accommodation early if you're travelling then.

Exploration

Places to Visit

El Salvador packs a surprising amount into a small country. Suchitoto is a beautifully preserved colonial town perched above Lago Suchitlán, perfect for a slow day of cobblestone wandering. The Ruta de las Flores winds through flower-draped mountain villages with excellent coffee and weekend markets. El Tunco and El Zonte are the go-to surf beaches on the coast. For nature lovers, Parque Nacional El Imposible and the crater lakes of Santa Ana volcano are unmissable.

Getting Around

How to Get Around

El Salvador is small enough to cover most of the country in a single day's drive. Chicken buses (repurposed American school buses) are the cheapest way to get between towns and are a cultural experience in themselves. For more comfort and flexibility, private shuttles are widely available and popular with backpackers. Renting a car is a great option if you want to explore off the beaten track — roads are generally decent and GPS works well. Uber operates in and around San Salvador.

Budget

How Much Does It Cost

El Salvador is one of the more affordable destinations in Central America. Budget travellers can get by on $30–45 USD per day covering a hostel dorm, local food, and buses. Mid-range travellers staying in guesthouses and eating at restaurants should budget $60–90 per day. El Salvador uses the US dollar as its official currency (alongside Bitcoin, which became legal tender in 2021), so there's no need to worry about exchange rates. Pupusas — the national dish — cost less than $1 each and are absolutely worth eating at every opportunity.

Experiences

Top Things to Do

Surf the black sand breaks at El Tunco, hike to the crater lake of Santa Ana volcano, and wander the indigo-painted streets of Suchitoto. Take a boat out onto Lago Suchitlán at sunset, explore the Joya de Cerén archaeological site (a Pompeii-like Maya village preserved under volcanic ash), and pick up handmade crafts along the Ruta de las Flores. Don't miss a morning at a local coffee farm in the highlands — El Salvador produces some excellent single-origin beans that rarely make it to export.

Staying Safe

Safety

El Salvador has undergone a dramatic transformation in recent years. Following a major government crackdown on gang activity beginning in 2022, crime rates have fallen sharply and the country now feels notably safer than it did even a few years ago. Tourist areas, beaches, and colonial towns are generally relaxed and welcoming. That said, it's still worth exercising common sense — avoid displaying expensive gear, stick to well-travelled routes after dark, and check current travel advisories before your trip. Most travellers report feeling comfortable and safe throughout their visit.

Essentials

Basic Facts

A quick reference for the practical things you'll want to know before you go.

Visa
Citizens of the US, EU, UK, Canada, and Australia can enter visa-free for up to 90 days. El Salvador is part of the CA-4 agreement, meaning you share a 90-day allowance across Guatemala, Honduras, and Nicaragua.
Language
Spanish is the official language. English is spoken in tourist areas and surf towns, but learning a few basics in Spanish goes a long way — locals genuinely appreciate the effort.
Currency
US Dollar (USD). Bitcoin is also legal tender since 2021. ATMs are widely available in cities and larger towns. Card payments accepted at most restaurants and hotels.
Capital
San Salvador
Time Zone
UTC−6 (Central Standard Time, no daylight saving)
Electricity
120V / 60Hz, Type A & B plugs (same as the US). No adapter needed for American devices.

Destinations › El Salvador › Itinerary

Itinerary

1–2 Weeks In El Salvador: A Complete Backpacking Itinerary

March 2026 · 12 min read · El Salvador

El Salvador is one of Central America's best kept secrets. It's tiny — you can drive coast to coast in under three hours — but it packs in volcanoes, surf beaches, colonial towns, and cloud forest all within reach of each other. Here's how I'd spend one to two weeks if I were doing it again.

Before you go: El Salvador is part of the CA-4 agreement. Your 90-day visa-free allowance is shared across Guatemala, Honduras, and Nicaragua — so if you're combining countries, keep track of your days.

The Route

Most travellers fly into San Salvador (SAL) and use the capital as a brief launching pad before heading out to the more interesting parts of the country. I'd recommend spending no more than a night or two in the city — it's worth seeing Mercado Central and the historic centre, but the real magic is elsewhere.

The route below works well as a loop: head west into the highlands and Ruta de las Flores first, then curve down to the coast, and finish in the north around Suchitoto before flying out. You can also run it in reverse.

One Week Itinerary

1
Arrive San Salvador — settle in, explore the centre
Land at SAL, grab a taxi or Uber into the city (around $15–20 USD). Check into your hostel in the Zona Rosa or San Benito neighbourhood — both are safe, walkable, and well-stocked with places to eat. In the afternoon, walk down to Plaza Barrios and the neoclassical Catedral Metropolitana. Eat pupusas for dinner. This is non-negotiable.
2
Santa Ana & Cerro Verde National Park
Take an early bus west to Santa Ana (about 1.5 hours, ~$1.50). The city has a beautiful neo-Gothic cathedral and a lively central market. In the afternoon, head up to Cerro Verde to hike around the rim of Lago Coatepeque — a stunning turquoise crater lake. Budget option: there are a few guesthouses on the lake's edge for a very reasonable price.
3
Hike Santa Ana Volcano
The hike to the summit of Santa Ana (Ilamatepec) is one of the best volcano hikes in Central America. It's about 2 hours up through cloud forest to the rim of a sulphurous crater lake. Guides are mandatory and depart from the park entrance at 11am. Wear layers — it gets cold near the top. Back in town, treat yourself to a cold Pilsener and a plate of yuca frita.
4–5
Ruta de las Flores
This scenic mountain route connects a string of small towns — Nahuizalco, Salcoatitán, Juayúa, Apaneca, and Ataco — each with its own character. Juayúa hosts a famous food festival every weekend. Ataco has the most Instagram-worthy murals and craft shops. Hire a tuk-tuk between towns or take the local buses. Stay two nights to do it properly — there are some excellent boutique guesthouses in Ataco.
6
El Tunco — Pacific Coast
Head south to the coast. El Tunco is the backpacker surf hub: black sand beach, consistent waves, cheap beer, and a relaxed vibe. It gets lively at night but is perfectly quiet during the day. If you don't surf, El Zonte (a 10-minute ride) is calmer and has a beautiful stretch of beach. Stay at least one night — sunsets here are extraordinary.
7
Suchitoto — then fly home
Make your way north to Suchitoto, El Salvador's most beautifully preserved colonial town. Blue and white cobblestone streets, a 19th-century church, and views over Lago Suchitlán. Walk down to the lake for a sunset boat ride if time allows. From here, it's a 45-minute drive back to San Salvador for your flight.

Got two weeks? Add two or three nights in Suchitoto, a day trip to the Cinquera cloud forest reserve, and an extra couple of days on the coast. You could also cross into Honduras for the Copán ruins and loop back.

Practical Notes

Getting around

Chicken buses between major towns cost $0.50–$2. Private shuttles (bookable through most hostels) run $10–20 per person between popular destinations and are worth it if you value time. Uber works well in and around San Salvador.

Where to stay

Hostels in El Salvador are excellent value — expect to pay $10–18 for a dorm bed, $30–50 for a private room. In Ataco, splurge on one of the boutique guesthouses if your budget allows; they're worth every dollar. On the coast, most accommodation is open-air and casual.

Budget

I comfortably travelled El Salvador on $40–50 USD per day including accommodation, food, transport, and activities. The country uses US dollars, so there's no currency headache. Tipping is appreciated but not obligatory — rounding up the bill is always welcome.

Safety

El Salvador is genuinely safe for travellers right now following the dramatic reduction in gang crime since 2022. I never felt unsafe anywhere on this route. Use common sense, avoid flashing expensive gear, and you'll be absolutely fine.

Last updated: March 2026 · Based on firsthand experience

← El Salvador

City Guide

The Ultimate Guide to Santa Ana, El Salvador's Second City

Volcanoes, crater lakes, Mayan ruins, and the best pupusas you'll ever eat — Santa Ana delivers on every front.

Mar 22, 2026

Getting to Santa Ana

I started my journey by flying in to the airport (SAL) in San Salvador. It is located about 45 minutes outside of the capital city itself. After taking a red-eye flight, I was so exhausted and headed directly to Santa Ana, the second largest city in the country. You can take a bus (with a transfer in San Salvador) or an Uber directly to Santa Ana. Santa Ana is also connected by tourist shuttles to Guatemala (Lake Atitlan & El Paredon) so it is a popular first-stop for many backpackers.

The Many Day Trips of Santa Ana

The main draw of coming to Santa Ana is that a great base for day trips in the surrounding area. Here are some of the top things to do:

Santa Ana Volcano (Ilamatepec)

The main reason why people come to Santa Ana is the volcano hike. With a bright turquoise volcanic lake at the top, it is a unique volcano experience that is hard to find elsewhere. The hike itself is not particularly challenging and takes approximately ~2hrs each way (4.4 mi / 7.1 km). Although Santa Ana is an active volcano, it is generally considered safe since it hasn't erupted since 2005 and authorities are constantly monitoring the volcano.

There are several ways to do it:

  • Book a tour — this is the easiest way to do the Santa Ana Volcano hike and usually comes bundled with a trip to Lago de Coatepeque (more on that later). I spent $20 for the tour and it was well worth it not having to worry about logistics. I'm sure there were more luxury tour options, but riding in the back of a pickup truck felt like a quintessential El Salvador experience. There are also tour options with pickup from other cities in El Salvador like San Salvador and El Tunco if you're not based in Santa Ana (link here)
  • DIY — the volcano is less than an hour outside of Santa Ana so you can easily access the volcano by car, public transit, uber or taxi. However, for safety reasons, the government of El Salvador requires you to take a guide while hiking up the volcano. It costs only $4 per person, but only at specific times during the day. Here is a link to a detailed guide with more logistical details on planning the hiking on your own.

Lago de Coatepeque

This is a deep blue crater lake, that lies only 45 minutes from the city center of Santa Ana. It is accessible by bus (take the #242 / #220 bus from Terminal Francisco Lara Pineda). The lake offers watersports like boats, jet skis and kayaks for rental.

My tour included a stop at Captain Morgan Hostel. The hostel had a restaurant with bar, complete with a deck to jump off of. It was a relaxing place to swim around and spend an afternoon. Captain Morgan Hostel is also a popular spot for travelers who want to spend a day to relax by the lake.

El Salto de Malacatiupán

Hotsprings + waterfalls, ¿por que no los dos? This is a truly unique experience that you only can find in El Salvador. Located between about an hour from Santa Ana (also an hour from Juayua), the El Salto de Malacatiupán waterfalls are basically nature's jacuzzi flowing through a stunning waterfall. They are very easily accessible by bus, car, uber or moped. However, they also remain undiscovered by most tourists as there are no tours leading there.

The entrance fee was $1 that you pay at a restaurant situated at the entrance. There is a short path that splits one side leading down to the entrance of the waterfall and one side the river that you can bathe in. The water is true jacuzzi temperature (37°C or 100°F)! There were not many other tourists when I was there, just some locals washing clothes down the river (which gave it a really relaxing feel). The whole trip can be done in a half day including transport.

Parque Arqueológico Tazumal

Located in the neighboring town only 30 minutes outside of Santa Ana, lies the ancient Mayan city of Chalchuapa. First inhabited by the Mayans in 250AD, it was later inhabited by the Toltec population until 1,200AD. Today, it stands as the largest set of Mayan Ruins in El Salvador. The complex is relatively large with a large pyramid in the center (and you might even spot some iguanas running around!)

You can easily access this Mayan archaeological site by taking the 202 bus out of Santa Ana or a ~$7 uber. The entrance fee was only a few dollars. There are tours offered in both Spanish and English for those who want more historical context and a small museum with some historical artifacts. The site is easily visited in an hour or so and Casa Blanca, another archaeological site, lies within a short walk from Tazumal.

Santa Ana — The City Itself

The city itself isn't very touristy and can easily be explored in 1 day. Here are the top things to do in the city:

Parque Libertad

The main square in Santa Ana which is home to many of the historic buildings and regional government buildings. Most of the main tourists sights in the city are centered around here.

  • Catedral de Nuestra Señora Santa Ana (Santa Ana Cathedral) — a beautiful white, neo-gothic cathedral built originally in 1575. It has a very intricate facade and is the most impressive piece of architecture that I saw in El Salvador. It remains an important centerpiece for the city with locals taking photos there and young kids playing with the pigeons
  • National Theater of Santa Ana — a historic theater built in 1910 lies only a few hundred meters from the main cathedral. The theatre is used to host national cultural events, is very well maintained and you can take a tour inside for $5
  • Alcaldía Municipal de Santa Ana and Monumento a la Libertad — Two beautiful government buildings around the square

Hector's Walking Tour

One of my favorite things to do in El Salvador was Hector's Walking Tour. Given all the recent changes in El Salvador's history, I was very interested in learning first hand from a local how the country had changed and what was life like before Bukele. Hector was the perfect guide for that. He led a very open ended tour (every day is different, depending on what the group wants to do).

We started at a popular coffee shop called Beats Coffee Centro Historico where we got to have El Salvador's best coffee. He honestly answered any and every question that our group had about El Salvador. It really opened my eyes to how rough El Salvador's past was with the Civil War in the 80s and gang violence. He described to us how El Salvadorans have adapted to the newfound feeling of safety and the cautiousness he has toward current politics and the future. Feeling a bit hungry around lunchtime, he led us to the local open air market where we sampled local dishes and fruits. The tour is completely tip based and is different every day. Link here.

Pupusa Making Class at Casa Coco

I signed up for the Pupusa Making class at my hostel and it was so good that I did it twice! Led by the lovely owner of the hostel named Yolanda, it was a few hours of making Pupusas from scratch. If you don't know, Pupusas are the national dish of El Salvador which are basically a really thick flour tortillas stuffed with any combination of stuffings. The most popular varieties are Revueltas meaning mixed with refried beans, Chicharrón and cheese as well as Loroco, a local herbal flower bud mixed with cheese.

The class is offered most days of the week (link here), lasts a few hours in the evening and costs $15. It was a really fun time complete with music and dancing. As a group of 8, we ended up making over 75 pupusas. Yolanda took me and one other traveler to give out our extras to the homeless.

Museo Regional de Occidente (Western Regional Museum)

The former mint for the El Salvadoran Colón before they adopted the U.S. Dollar as their main currency in 2001. It has now been transformed into the main historical museum in Santa Ana. I can't personally recommend the museum for everyone. There were some ancient artifacts and it explained the history of the Santa Ana region. The exhibits seemed a bit underfunded and the exhibits were all in Spanish. For only $3 entrance, I can't complain too much.

Old Art School

Located a bit further south outside of downtown Santa Ana, there are the ruins of an Old Art School. Once the vibrant center of creativity for Santa Ana, the Mariano Mendez Art School was abandoned. Popular with photographers, the art school serves as a reminder of Santa Ana's rich cultural heritage. Unfortunately, I showed up without a permit so I couldn't explore the site itself. A permit can be easily acquired from the local tourist office, but requires some advance planning.

Where to Eat!

Breakfast, lunch and dinner — El Salvadorans love their pupusas! You can find them on almost every street corner and I was never disappointed. However, there are many other dishes to try. Here were some of my favorite places to eat in Santa Ana:

  • Pupusería La Ceiba — considered the best pupuseria in Santa Ana!
  • Comedor y Pupuseria Claudia — a local spot offering a variety of dishes and pupusas
  • Azados — BBQ every Sunday — it may not look like much on google maps, but this was one of my favorite meals in El Salvador. Every Sunday, this family has a bbq and a large plate is only $5
  • Beats Coffee Centro Historico — home to an nationally recognized barista, this is a great place to sample some of El Salvador's best coffee
  • Karlita Café — a bakery / cafe which served a variety of interesting breakfast options
  • Street Stands around Parque Libertad — very cheap option (if you're feeling a bit adventurous!)

Places to Stay

There are many wonderful places to stay in Santa Ana ranging from hostels to hotels to luxury hotels. Note that many places in El Salvador only offer cold water showers so be prepared!

Hostels

Casa Coco — I stayed here personally and had a wonderful time. Casa Coco is a small hostel with a strong communal vibe. The owner, Yolanda, was very sweet and welcoming. The hostel offered a lot of tours (Santa Ana Volcano and 7 waterfalls) and activities (pupusa making class) all for a fair price. I had a wonderful time here.

Rick's Hostel — They have two locations: 1 in Santa Ana and 1 in Juayua — Ruta de Las Flores. The hostel offers motorbike rentals for $15 a day. They also have a service where they will transport your bags from one location to another if you want to make the journey between the two cities by moped. I ran into the owner (not named Rick!) a couple times on my trip, but a very friendly guy. rickshostels.com
